source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"This pattern is most consistent with uncomplicated dementia progression, because dementia commonly changes markedly over hours within the same day.","B":"This pattern is most consistent with normal cognitive aging, because fluctuating attention and sudden confusion are expected during hospitalization.","C":"This pattern is most consistent with delirium, an acute disturbance that warrants prompt evaluation for an underlying medical or medication-related cause.","D":"This pattern is most consistent with major depression alone, because depression typically causes abrupt disorientation and fluctuating attention over hours."}}
source_row.rationale: Delirium is characterized by an acute change in attention and cognition with a fluctuating course. Option C is correct because the sudden, variable confusion warrants evaluation for an underlying medical or medication-related cause. Option A incorrectly describes the abrupt hourly fluctuation as uncomplicated dementia progression. Option B incorrectly normalizes sudden confusion as expected aging or hospitalization. Option D attributes the pattern to depression alone even though abrupt disorientation and fluctuating attention point to delirium.
source_row.source_detail: Continuing Education/Introduction and Evaluation/DSM criteria: delirium is an acute disturbance of attention/awareness and cognition developing over a short period with a fluctuating course; evaluate for underlying medical, medication, substance, or environmental causes. StatPearls Delirium updated 2026-01-10; current NCBI Bookshelf version rechecked 2026-08-15. source_row.stem: A hospitalized 78-year-old develops abrupt confusion, impaired attention, and disorganized thinking that fluctuate over the course of the day. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
